(b) Wire client R1/R2 in Vizor: on startup or poll open, for a proxy-enabled ACTIVE round where the participation reader shows spent governance nullifiers but there is no local proxy state, run proxy::recover and redeliver. (c) Reword C8 and the reinstall row to say the delegation counts once Vizor has finished sending it, and that reopening Vizor finishes sending it. A wakelock is optional polish.

findings.title: A locked multi-bundle allocation can strand unexecuted bundles with no exit
findings.description: Allocations lock at the first broadcast (clear_proxy_allocation is refused once any proxy POST is reserved). Execution is atomic per bundle only, and on mobile it can be interrupted between bundles. Before each bundle is proved, the client re-checks every chosen delegate and blocks the bundle (ProxyBlocked::DelegateChanged) if the delegate is frozen, suspended, revoked or has a pending key change. A bundle whose proxy batch is undispatched or in flight is 'held', so no own cast can be planned on it. Vizor marks a chain rejection terminal for that VAN. No specified operation lets the user re-target the slots that never executed, convert them to Keep, or vote with them. Re-planning those slots would not violate decision 2, because they were never delegated.
findings.evidence: [doc] integrated-design-v1.md:171,182; specs/client.md:121 (committed -> locked), :306 (mutual exclusion / held_bundles), :505 (entry changed between commit and proving: block; 'can be cleared while nothing is dispatched'), :507 (terminal rejection; after 3 rejections ChainTerminal), :512 (clear refused once any POST is reserved); specs/vizor.md:497-518 (REJECTED terminal for that VAN; Discard refused after broadcast); specs/client.md:192-198 (case c splits one delegate across b0 and b1).
findings.failure_scenario: Two bundles, 'everything 60/40'. The planner gives A: b0 4,000 + b1 800 and B: b1 3,200. Bundle 0 is broadcast, then the phone backgrounds. Before resume, B pauses themselves (freeze), is coordinator-suspended, or starts a 72 h co-signed DIK change. The pre-prove check blocks b1, the allocation cannot be cleared, and b1 is held, so the user cannot vote with it either. All of b1's weight (including A's 800) abstains on every proposal. The same dead end follows three terminal rejections of b1's batch.
findings.proposed_fix: Add an explicit 'replan undispatched' operation. Once any bundle is final, slots whose bundle has no landed or in-flight tx can be re-targeted or turned into Keep, with a new plan_digest generation. Finality applies only to landed DCs. Release held bundles on terminal rejection. To shrink the window, prove every bundle's batch before broadcasting any of them, then broadcast back to back.

verdict.reasoning:
The spec has no exit from this state. clear_proxy_allocation is refused allocation-wide once any proxy POST is reserved. A bundle with an undispatched proxy batch is 'held', so no cast is planned on it. ProxyBlocked::DelegateChanged proceeds only on a continuity-signed rotation, and clearing is allowed only while nothing is dispatched. ChainTerminal after 3 rejections does not specify releasing the hold. Freeze can be undone by unfreeze, and a co-signed key change may unblock after 72 h, but suspension, revocation, a change still pending at round end, and ChainTerminal all leave the bundle stranded until vote end.

The window is small in the normal path, because v5 overlaps up to five bundles and the pre-prove checks run close together. It is reachable when mobile backgrounding or a crash interrupts execution between bundles, and on repeated chain rejection of one bundle. The consequence is the user's whole bundle abstaining, with no user action available. That is a real state-machine gap that needs a defined exit before implementation. Releasing undispatched slots does not conflict with decision 2, because those DCs never landed.
verdict.evidence: [doc] specs/client.md:121 (committed -> locked), :306 (held bundles, mutual exclusion), :505 (DelegateChanged; clear only while nothing is dispatched), :507 (3 rejections -> ChainTerminal; no release specified), :512 (clear refused once any POST is reserved), :192-198 (case c splits one delegate across b0 and b1); [doc] specs/vizor.md:503,518 (REJECTED terminal for that VAN; Discard refused after broadcast); [doc] zcash_voting docs/migrating-to-v5.md:248-250 (default execution overlaps five bundles, which narrows but does not close the window); [doc] integrated-design-v1.md:118,126,182 (freeze/revoke/suspension; client refuses non-ACTIVE or pending-change delegates).
verdict.refined_fix: Add a per-bundle release in the client: when a bundle is ProxyBlocked{DelegateChanged} without continuity, or ChainTerminal, and none of its proxy batches has a reserved POST or a landed tx, allow release_proxy_bundle(bundle). It drops that bundle's undispatched slots, turns their weight into Keep (lifting the hold so own casts can be planned), and records a new plan_digest generation for audit. Landed slots stay final. Vizor surfaces it as 'This part of your delegation couldn't be sent. Vote with it yourself.' Re-targeting to other delegates can wait for top-up support (see LIV-5).

findings.title: Three incompatible DC cutoffs, no chain backstop, and device-clock timing
findings.description: The integrated design is internally inconsistent. Section 4.4 has no chain deadline, but the client 'blocks new delegation inside the helper last-moment buffer' (40% of the round, capped at 6 h) with a hard cutoff 30 min before end. Section 2 step 4 still expects last-moment single-share DCs. The Vizor spec allows delegation until vote_end_time minus 10 min. The chain spec stores cutoff = vote_end - clamp(10%, 60 s, 1 h). Taken literally, section 4.4 blocks the last 6 h of a 7-day round (when informed delegation matters most) and about 40% plus 30 min of a short [TEST] round. Without a chain cutoff, the client is the only guard, and it uses the device clock. The 'expired' check runs only before broadcast. A DC that lands too late for its single share is accepted and the VAN is spent. The chain spec's cutoff would instead reject the tx and leave the VAN intact.
findings.evidence: [doc] integrated-design-v1.md:32, :161-163, :259 (O3); specs/vizor.md:168,288 (end - 10 min); specs/chain.md:18, :586-589 and :591-599 (weight-loss case 1 depends on the stored cutoff); [code] Vizor _nowSeconds = DateTime.now() (lib/src/providers/voting/voting_session_provider.dart:4308-4310) feeds is_last_moment (zcash_voting vote_work/mod.rs:118-135); [code] helper retryCutoff gives only an immediate attempt when 30 s or less remains (internal/helper/retry_schedule.go:68-83); [doc] vizor.md:504 EXPIRED only 'before broadcast'.
findings.failure_scenario: A desktop clock is 15 min slow, or a mobile proof built at T-20 min is broadcast at T-40 s after the app was backgrounded. The chain accepts the DC (no cutoff), and in single-share mode 100% of w rides on one share. The helper gets one attempt at the end-of-round queue, misses vote_end_time, and the whole DC is lost silently. A chain cutoff would have rejected the tx, leaving the user able to vote directly.
findings.proposed_fix: Resolve O3 in favor of the chain spec's stored cutoff_time as the consensus backstop. Make every client derive 'now' and the cutoff from the latest chain block time, warning when the device clock is skewed by more than 60 s, and re-check before broadcast. State one rule in all docs: standard layout before the last-moment window, single-share from the window start until cutoff_time, and no DCs after it. Drop the separate 30 min and 10 min client constants.

verdict.reasoning:
The docs do disagree. Integrated §4.4 says the client 'blocks new delegation inside the helper last-moment buffer, with a hard cutoff 30 min before end', which conflicts with its own §2 step 4 and client §3.3 (single-share DCs in the last-moment window). Vizor uses end - 10 min. The chain spec stores cutoff = end - clamp(10%, 60 s, 1 h). One rule is needed.

The rest is weaker than claimed. The chain-versus-no-chain question is already tracked as O3. The intended reading of §4.4 is clear from step 4 and client §3.3, so an implementer would not ship a 6 h block. The 'silent loss' scenario (single-share DC broadcast at T-40 s) is the same risk a last-moment direct vote carries today. A chain cutoff would reject that DC, but the user's fallback, a direct vote at T-40 s, faces the same helper deadline. So the chain cutoff is not clearly better. The device-clock timing in Vizor and the before-broadcast-only expiry check are pre-existing vote behavior. The helper still makes a first attempt for an immediately submitted share until vote_end.
verdict.evidence: [doc] integrated-design-v1.md:32 (single-share DCs), :161-163 (§4.4 wording), :259 (O3 already open); [doc] specs/client.md:221 (last-moment DCs use the single-share layout, as votes do); [doc] specs/vizor.md:168,288 (end - 10 min), :504 (EXPIRED only before broadcast); [doc] specs/chain.md:18,586-589; [code] vizor voting_session_provider.dart:4308-4310 (DateTime.now, also used for votes); [code] zcash_voting vote_work/mod.rs:118-135; [code] vote-sdk internal/helper/retry_schedule.go:68-83 (first attempt allowed when 30 s or less remains).
verdict.refined_fix: Close O3 with one sentence used verbatim in the integrated, chain, client and Vizor specs. Standard layout before the last-moment window; single-share layout from the window start until a single client cutoff constant; no client DCs after it. Then either adopt the chain spec's stored cutoff_time as the consensus backstop, and set the client constant to that same time, or explicitly keep vote parity with no chain cutoff. Remove the conflicting 'blocks new delegation inside the helper last-moment buffer' phrase and the separate 10 min and 30 min constants. Deriving 'now' from the latest chain block time is a reasonable improvement, but it is pre-existing vote behavior and optional here.

findings.title: 'Delegate more' (Vizor v1) conflicts with the client's single locked allocation per round
findings.description: The integrated rule 'delegation available until first own cast' and Vizor's 'Delegate more' (a second batch from the successor VAN, up to 10 delegates in total) need several commits per round. The client spec defers top-ups to v1.1 and models one allocation per (round, wallet) that becomes locked, plus at most one slot per (bundle, delegate). Shipping Vizor's flow on that schema either fails at the second commit or rewrites a locked plan_digest. The second option breaks the guarantee that what the user confirmed is what executes, and it breaks recovery, which inserts recovered rows as state = locked.
findings.evidence: [doc] specs/vizor.md:249,442 ('Delegate more'); specs/client.summary.md:46 (not in v1, one committed allocation per round); specs/client.md:351 PRIMARY KEY (round_id, wallet_id), :375 UNIQUE (round_id, wallet_id, bundle_index, delegate_index), :497 (recovered allocation state locked); integrated-design-v1.md:205.
findings.failure_scenario: A user delegates 50% to A, then taps 'Delegate more' to add B, or to top up A, before voting. commit_proxy_allocation conflicts on the locked row, so the user is stuck on an unexplained error with the kept weight. Alternatively, an ad hoc fix overwrites the locked plan and its digest, and a later crash or R1 recovery cannot reconcile the slots.
findings.proposed_fix: Decide before implementation. If top-ups stay in v1, model allocations as append-only generations keyed by (round, wallet, generation), each with its own plan_digest. Allow a second slot for the same delegate on the same bundle (or merge top-ups into new slots), and count the 10-delegate cap across generations. Otherwise remove 'Delegate more' from Vizor v1.

verdict.reasoning:
There is a direct contradiction between two specs that the integrated design both calls authoritative. The Vizor spec ships 'Delegate more' in v1: a second batch from the successor VAN, existing rows locked, up to 10 delegates in total. The client spec defers top-ups to v1.1. It models one allocation per (round, wallet) with state committed -> locked, allows at most one slot per (bundle, delegate), and has recovery insert allocations as locked. Client.md §3.1 even says slots 'may be added to the same remainder VAN later', but the schema has no way to represent a second commit.

Integrated §7 ('available until first own cast') is ambiguous between the two. Built as specified, a Vizor 'Delegate more' would hit a primary-key or uniqueness conflict, or would need to rewrite a locked plan_digest. The damage is integration failure or unclear UX, not silent weight loss. It still needs a v1 scope decision before implementation.
verdict.evidence: [doc] specs/vizor.md:249,258,442,807 ('Delegate more' in v1 screens and CTAs); [doc] specs/client.summary.md:46 (OQ4: not in v1, one committed allocation per round); [doc] specs/client.md:116-121 (committed -> locked; one slot per (bundle, delegate)), :128 (slots may be added later), :351 (PRIMARY KEY (round_id, wallet_id)), :375 (UNIQUE (round_id, wallet_id, bundle_index, delegate_index)), :497 (recovered rows locked); [doc] integrated-design-v1.md:205.
verdict.refined_fix: Make the decision in the integrated design. The minimal option is to adopt client OQ4 for v1: remove 'Delegate more' from Vizor v1 (PD-1 state and CTA), and restate §7 as 'delegation is available until the first proxy dispatch or own cast in the round'. If top-ups must ship in v1, key allocations by (round, wallet, generation) with a per-generation plan_digest. Drop the (bundle, delegate) uniqueness, or key slots by generation. Count the 10-delegate cap across generations, and have recovery reconstruct generations from the hint order.

findings.title: 10-minute directory freshness makes the directory a liveness single point of failure for delegators
findings.description: Review blocks unless the signed directory snapshot is no more than 10 minutes old, and gate G6 fails closed. For delegation safety, only the chain record (index, DIK/DRK, status) matters, and it is IAVL-proved immediately before proving. Impersonation takedowns are on-chain coordinator suspensions, which that proof already reflects. Under the current rule, an outage of both directory mirrors blocks every new delegation, even near the deadline when demand is highest.
findings.evidence: [doc] specs/vizor.md:49 (G6), :192 (refresh if older than 10 min), :280 (registryStale blocks the CTA); integrated-design-v1.md:182 (chain authoritative; cross-checked before proving), :212; specs/identity.md:584-588 (profiles doc expiry 30 h).
findings.failure_scenario: In the last day of a round, the valargroup directory host and functions.vizor.cash are both down for an hour (a shared CDN or DNS issue). Every Vizor delegator hits 'The delegate list is out of date', although the vote chain RPC is up and the delegate's chain record verifies.
findings.proposed_fix: Keep the fresh IAVL chain-record proof as the blocking check. Accept any signed, unexpired snapshot (up to 24-30 h) with a 'profile info may be out of date' banner. Let the exact #index or deep-link path work from the chain record plus the fingerprint alone.

verdict.reasoning:
The 10-minute rule is real. If both mirrors fail at review time, new delegation is blocked even though the chain RPC is up.

The finding's premise that 'for delegation safety, only the chain record matters' is wrong for this design. Several blocking signals exist only in the signed directory: proof 'removed', X account 'suspended', impersonation_confirmed (hidden, published within 15 min of moderation while coordinator suspension follows a 24 h triage), lookalike_of, and the verifier-compromise playbook's 'verification under review' flag. Accepting a 24-30 h snapshot when refresh fails would let an outage, or a deliberate DoS of both mirrors during a takedown, suppress exactly those signals. So the fail-closed rule is deliberate and the proposed fix is not materially better.

What is left is a minor liveness tradeoff. It needs a two-mirror outage, loses no weight, and leaves direct voting available. The 10-min threshold is also stricter than the identity spec's 15-min wallet refresh cadence; aligning the two is a nit.

Optionally soften liveness: when refresh fails, accept a verified cached snapshot no older than a short bound (for example 1 h, or the 15-min cadence plus margin), with a 'Delegate list may be out of date' banner. Only do this for entries that are listed or featured with no flags and that predate the round. Block brand-new or lookalike-flagged entries. Add a third mirror on independent infrastructure. Do not extend acceptance to the 30 h profiles expiry.

findings.title: Copy C9 invites a per-proposal mental model for a delegation that covers every proposal
findings.description: Delegation covers the whole round: the delegate votes the delegated weight on every proposal, and the user's own votes use only the kept weight. C9 reads 'Don't want to vote on every proposal? Delegate some or all…', which suggests delegating just the proposals the user skips. Because delegation is final, a user who delegates everything expecting to still vote on one proposal loses their voice on it.
findings.evidence: [doc] specs/vizor.md:797 (C9), :788 (C1), :247 (order rule); integrated-design-v1.md:8 (decision 2).
findings.failure_scenario: A user sees the C9 card, delegates everything to @alice to 'skip the boring ones', then opens P3 to vote and finds no weight left. They cannot undo it, and @alice votes the opposite way on P3.
findings.proposed_fix: Reword C9, for example 'Your delegate votes for you on every proposal in this round'. On review, list every proposal the delegation covers. In the combined review, state that the user's own votes use only the kept amount and do not replace the delegate's vote.

findings.title: Cross-install and same-seed cases surface only as post-proof rejections, and kept weight is tied to one install
findings.description: Vizor's alreadyVoted comes from the local SDK database. A second install on the same seed (desktop plus phone, old Vizor, Zodl) offers delegation, the user proves ZKP1+ZKP4, and the chain rejects the tx because the governance nullifiers are spent. If two installs bundled differently, some bundles can land while others are rejected, so the executed split differs from the confirmed one. Kept weight can only be voted from the install holding the round hotkey. Vizor scopes hotkey storage keys by account UUID, so R1 (DB lost, hotkey kept) is effectively unreachable after a reinstall or restore. Only R2 applies, and it cannot vote the remainder.

On desktop, Vizor shows 'Delegate voting power', and the user spends minutes proving before getting 'The voting chain rejected this delegation'. Or the user kept 25% to vote later, switches to a new phone, and finds the kept 25% cannot be voted.

If the nullifiers are spent and there is no local state, run R2 and show 'Delegated from another device' with the recovered delegations. Add copy telling users that kept ZEC must be voted from the same device before the round ends.

findings.title: The helper checks the mutable delegate index before proving it has seen the DC leaf
findings.description: Helper ingest runs validateShareChoice before verifyCommitment. The current choice check reads immutable round config. The proposal-0 branch will read the mutable NextDelegateIndex. A helper whose node lags the head could return a permanent 400 for a valid DC share to a just-registered delegate, before checking that it even has the DC leaf. The client treats a 400 as non-transient for that helper. Other helpers usually cover the share, but in a small fleet this can strand shares.
findings.evidence: [code] vote-sdk internal/helper/api.go:336-337 (validateShareChoice) precedes api.go:366-367 (verifyCommitment); cmd/svoted/cmd/helper.go:310-341 (current check uses immutable round proposals); [code] zcash_voting helper/client.rs:1737-1741 (400 is not transient); [doc] integrated-design-v1.md:167.
findings.failure_scenario: A delegate registers at height h. A delegator delegates immediately, and the DC lands at h+2. Two of the five target helpers run on nodes still at h-1, and they permanently reject that DC's shares with 'unknown delegate'.
findings.proposed_fix: For proposal_id 0, run verifyCommitment first: a present leaf proves the helper's height is at least the DC height, which is at least the registration height. Alternatively, return 503 (retryable) when the index is at or above the helper's NextDelegateIndex but the leaf is missing.

findings.title: Pending key changes and freeze semantics block delegations, and the unfreeze rule is inconsistent
findings.description: The client refuses delegates with any pending change. A routine 72 h co-signed DIK change therefore blocks all new delegations to that delegate, and all not-yet-proved bundles of existing allocations (LIV-3), for 3 days. A 7-day recover_identity started after an X takeover does the same until the delegate notices and cancels, and Vizor has no push to tell them. The integrated design also says freeze and unfreeze can be signed by DIK or DRK, while the identity spec allows unfreezing only through a DIK-signed DRK rotation. If a DRK can unfreeze, a thief holding it can undo the owner's freeze.
findings.evidence: [doc] integrated-design-v1.md:115-118 (freeze/unfreeze DIK or DRK), :182 (refuse pending-change); specs/identity.md:110-118 (freeze undone only by DIK rotation; change 72 h; recover 7 d); specs/vizor.md:285 (delegateUnavailable includes key change pending).
findings.failure_scenario: A popular delegate moves the DIK to cold storage 4 days into a 7-day round. For the remaining 3 days, Vizor shows '@alice isn't accepting delegations', and in-flight second bundles of her delegators stay blocked.
findings.proposed_fix: Block new delegations only for an uncosigned pending recover_identity. Allow them during a co-signed change, with a banner. The pool follows the index, and routes use the effective key. Remove the DRK 'unfreeze' op to match the identity spec. Surface any pending recovery prominently on the delegate dashboard, plus an optional verifier-sent notice to the bound X, GitHub or domain identity.

findings.title: All-or-nothing route batches make retries near the deadline fragile
findings.description: A MsgDelegateRoute is rejected whole if any listed proposal is already routed. After an ambiguous broadcast (an ingress timeout or a lost response), a retry that adds proposals fails with ErrDelegateRouteExists. The delegate's UI also times the deadline from the device clock.
findings.evidence: [doc] specs/chain.md:277-290 (one-shot; ErrDelegateRouteExists for any routed p); integrated-design-v1.md:124; [code] device-clock time source (voting_session_provider.dart:4308-4310).
findings.failure_scenario: At T-3 min the delegate routes P1-P5, and the response times out although the tx landed. The delegate adds P6 and retries P1-P6. The batch is rejected as 'already routed', and by the time the wallet refreshes and resubmits P6, the round has closed. P6 abstains for the whole pool.
findings.proposed_fix: Have the chain treat entries identical to stored routes (same p and decision) as no-ops and reject only conflicting ones. Alternatively, have the client always re-fetch the route set and submit only the unrouted delta. Show the route deadline from chain time with a safety margin.

findings.title: Gates and kill switches must never stop work after commit or broadcast
findings.description: Gates G2 (remote kill switch) and G5 (capabilities and VK fingerprint, failing when 'absent or unreachable') hide the feature for a round. The never-hide rule covers status views only. If the job or driver checks the same gate before running ProxyDelegate on remaining bundles, or SubmitProxyShares and ConfirmProxyShare, a mid-round kill switch or an unreachable capabilities endpoint halts delivery for DCs already on chain.
findings.evidence: [doc] specs/vizor.md:45 (G2 hides new delegations), :48 (G5 absent or mismatch: hidden for that round), :53 (never-hide covers status, results and poll card only).
findings.failure_scenario: Ops flips the remote flag off mid-round because of a UI bug. A user whose DC landed but whose shares were not yet delivered (LIV-2) reopens Vizor, the gated driver skips proxy steps, and the DC weight never reaches the pool.
findings.proposed_fix: Specify that G1-G7 control only previewing and committing new allocations. Once an allocation is committed, and always after the first broadcast, proxy steps, share delivery and R2 run regardless of gates. Add a test where the kill switch is off with an in-flight DC.

Binding to the numeric X user id instead of the handle is correct. Using oEmbed only for re-verification, only when the handle matches the last handle confirmed through the API, and never for new registrations, is a sound use of a published interface. Excluding the syndication endpoint matches the X ToS.
attestation_id is single-use, and the DIK and DRK sign a reg digest bound to that attestation_id and subject_commit, so a valid attestation cannot be front-run onto another key or replayed.
Accepting proposal-0 reveals for any existing index regardless of delegate status is correct. The chain cannot see d at DC time, so rejecting reveals would strand weight instead of protecting it.

Revocation by the DIK is immediate and terminal, so whoever holds the current DIK can always end an entry before a hostile co-signed change takes effect (IDN-6 covers the case where only the DRK is held).

findings.title: A hijacked X account or a compromised verifier can take over a delegate index in the middle of a round, and removing the verifier does not stop recoveries that are already pending
findings.description: Pools follow the index, and delegation is final. A verifier-attested recovery (7 d delay) installs new keys, and those keys can route every proposal the delegate has not yet routed in every active round. Round lengths are 1 week to 3 months, so a recovery can be started and can take effect inside one round. The only defence is the owner cancelling within the delay. Non-featured entries get no manual review. Dormant or travelling owners will miss it. The identity spec admits that "an inattentive owner could lose the entry". Separately, `Effective()` turns a pending recovery into live keys purely by time. It never re-checks that the verifiers who attested it are still in the current set. So the containment step in the playbook (the coordinator removes the compromised verifier key) leaves every recovery already submitted under that key to take effect.

[doc] identity.md:114 (recovery 7 d, cancellable only by the owner), :132 ("nobody cancels, so it takes effect after 7 d"), :399-405 (Effective() checks time only), :907-908 (playbook relies on owners cancelling), identity.summary.md:57. integrated-design-v1.md:2,115,130 (final delegation; recover_identity; pools keyed by index).
findings.failure_scenario: Round R (2 weeks) starts on day 0, and @alice (listed, not featured) receives delegations on days 0-5. On day 3 an attacker phishes her X account, posts a marker for DIK_a, gets a RECOVER attestation (no review for non-featured entries) and submits recover_identity. It becomes effective on day 10. Alice does not cancel. On day 10 one MsgDelegateRoute from the attacker routes all of R's unrouted proposals, and those routes are final. Variant: a misused verifier key submits recoveries for 500 dormant entries, and coordinators remove the key on day 1. All 500 still activate on day 7, because Effective() does not consult the verifier set.

Keys installed by recover_identity cannot route rounds created before the recovery took effect. In those rounds the pool abstains instead of being stolen. (2) Store the attesting verifier_ids in `pending`. When the recovery would take effect, void it unless recover_threshold is still met by verifiers in the current set. (3) Launch with recover_threshold=2: the online Valar key plus a second key behind two-person manual approval. Recoveries are rare. (4) Show pending-recovery banners to delegators of active rounds and push-notify the delegate's own device.

It is cancellable only by the owner, Vizor specs no notification, and Effective() activates on time alone and sets status ACTIVE. Routes stay accepted until vote_end, so a recovery started inside a 2-week round can take effect and route that round. Existing mitigations reduce exposure but do not remove it. Wallets refuse new delegations to entries with a pending change, the listing drops to lookup_only, and a key_mismatch flag appears. Delegations made before the recovery started are final and still exposed. The verifier-removal variant also holds. Coordinator suspension (reason 4) is the only other containment, and it cannot void the pending change. So after review a legitimate owner's entry ends up either suspended for good or controlled by the attacker. The spec itself concedes that 'an inattentive owner could lose the entry'.

Reject a MsgDelegateRoute for round R when R.created_at < recovered_at, including routes signed by keys that the recovered DIK rotates in later. Unrouted proposals in those rounds abstain. Co-signed changes are unaffected. (2) Store the attesting verifier_ids in `pending`. Effective() activates only if at least recover_threshold of them are still in the current verifier set; otherwise it drops the pending change, so removing a verifier key voids its in-flight recoveries. (3) Vizor: show a blocking pending-recovery banner on the delegate's own home screen when the app opens, and on delegators' status screens for active-round delegations. recover_threshold=2 at launch is optional hardening.

findings.title: The isolated attest-signer will sign any digest the internet-facing API sends it, and the compromise alarm reads a table that the API itself writes
findings.description: The verifier is 1-of-1 at launch. The attest-signer receives an opaque `(attest digest, issuance record id)` from verifier-api and signs it, so the HSM protects only against key extraction. If verifier-api is compromised (it is internet-facing and parses X, GitHub, DNS and oEmbed HTML), it becomes a signing oracle: up to 200 signatures an hour and 2,000 a day, for any REGISTER or RECOVER on any index. The detection control, "on-chain registration whose attestation_id is missing from issuances", compares against the Postgres `issuances` table. The API writes that table ahead of each signature, so a compromised API simply writes the matching rows and the alarm never fires. The publisher shares the same database. Forged registrations bound to a real person's X id would therefore also be published as listed profiles.
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:457-458 (signer accepts the digest), :471 and :884 (alarm keyed on issuances), :498 (API writes issuances ahead of signing), :459-470 (one shared store for the API, publisher and indexer). integrated-design-v1.md:193 (1-of-1 at launch).
findings.failure_scenario: The attacker gets remote code execution in a verifier-api container. For each target index it inserts `issuances(kind=RECOVER, state=issued)` and posts a RECOVER attest digest over the API's mTLS identity. The signer signs. The attacker submits recover_identity for 100 delegates. The chain-indexer finds a matching issuance for each and does not page anyone. The outcome is IDN-1 at scale.
findings.proposed_fix: Have the signer receive the structured fields, recompute the `attest` digest itself, and enforce its own invariants against its own chain replica: RECOVER subject_commit equals the entry's, a per-index cooldown, and featured entries refused. Keep the signer's log separate from the API's database. Reconcile chain events against the signer log and against an independent re-fetch of the proof post, not against `issuances`. Combine with recover_threshold=2 (IDN-1). Give the publisher its own read-only replica.

verdict.reasoning: The signer accepts an opaque digest from the API, and the only compromise alarm compares chain events with the `issuances` table that the API writes ahead of each signature. A compromised verifier-api (or its mTLS client credentials plus database role) is therefore a signing oracle that the alarm cannot see. With 1-of-1 at launch, forged REGISTERs can bind real famous X ids. The publisher shares the store and hydrates the real handle and avatar from X, so the result is a convincing listed impostor. The proposed reconciliation 'against the signer log' only detects key theft: under API compromise the signer did sign, so its log matches. The only independent signal today is the refresher's weekly proof recheck. That runs in the same trust domain and feeds the listing state, not a page.

For RECOVER, and for REGISTER of subjects above a follower threshold, it re-fetches the proof post with its own X credentials before signing. It enforces its own per-kind budgets (RECOVER far below REGISTER), a per-index cooldown and a featured-entry refusal, using its own chain view. Page on-call when an independent re-verification (separate credentials and a read-only DB role) fails for any registration or recovery seen on chain within 24 h, and on any chain-observed RECOVER spike. Signer-log reconciliation catches only key theft. Give the publisher a read-only replica.

findings.title: Coordinators can in effect re-key any delegate and censor delegates in the middle of a round, and the threshold defaults to 1
findings.description: The design says coordinator suspension "cannot create entries, change keys, or void routes". However, `MsgSetProxyDelegationParams` (identity: `MsgSetProxyDelegateParams`) lets the same coordinator set: (a) replace the verifier set and recover_threshold; (b) set `identity_recovery_delay_secs` and `identity_change_delay_secs`, with no consensus floor. Coordinator actions use one global threshold, which defaults to 1, and threshold-1 actions execute inside the proposing tx. A single coordinator key can therefore install its own verifier, set the recovery delay to 0, recover any delegate, and route its pools in active rounds right away. Today a coordinator cannot redirect votes in an active round, so this is a real expansion of trust. Suspension is also immediate and round-agnostic. A coordinator quorum (or one key at threshold 1) can suspend chosen delegates shortly before vote_end, and their unrouted pools abstain. Delegators cannot react because delegation is final.

In the next blocks: submit recover_identity for the 30 featured delegates (each effective immediately), then send MsgDelegateRoute for every active round. All routes are final before anyone reacts. Alternatively: suspend the five largest delegates (by visible share count) one hour before vote_end with reason 1.
findings.proposed_fix: (1) Put hard minimums in consensus: recovery delay ≥ 7 d and change delay ≥ 72 h, not settable lower by params. (2) A verifier added by params can attest only after it has been in the set longer than the recovery delay. (3) Require at least 2 approvals for verifier/params/suspension payloads regardless of the global threshold. (4) Suspension blocks routes only in rounds created after it, or takes effect after a public 24-72 h notice. Impersonation inside the current round is better handled by wallets blocking new delegation. (5) State the coordinator trust model in ZIP-DR.

verdict.reasoning: The core holds. Params can replace the verifier set, set thresholds and set the identity delays with no consensus floor, so 'suspension is the coordinators' only power over an entry' is false. Production has exactly one vote manager, so threshold-1 execution inside the proposing tx is the real deployed state. The claim of a 'real expansion of trust' is overstated, though. That same single key can already schedule an x/upgrade with arbitrary Info, and production validators run Cosmovisor with auto-download enabled, so a compromised coordinator key is already catastrophic. The new delta is a silent, non-halting path, which still deserves floors. Fix (4) is counterproductive. Immediate suspension is what makes deceived delegators' pools abstain instead of being routed by an impostor. Delaying it, or limiting it to future rounds, hands the current round to the impostor. Fix (3) cannot be met until more vote managers exist. The chain spec already made the recovery delay a constant, which supports fix (1).

verdict.refined_fix: (1) Consensus floors: recovery delay ≥ 7 d and co-signed change delay ≥ 72 h, as constants or param minimums that params cannot lower. (2) A newly added verifier key may attest only after it has been in the set longer than the recovery delay (store added_at). (3) Keep suspension immediate. State in ZIP-DR that coordinators are fully trusted (they can already push binaries via x/upgrade), and that moving to more vote managers with threshold ≥2 is an ops prerequisite. Drop the delayed or future-round-only suspension proposal.

That key sits in KMS used by the publisher, on the same infrastructure as the verifier. Curator 2-of-3 approval happens in the admin console, and wallets cannot verify it. The playbook calls a forged snapshot "presentation-only lies". Delegators choose by handle, avatar and the Featured badge, and their delegation is final, so relabelling is enough to divert weight. The second mirror is a pull-through cache of the primary, not an independent publisher.

findings.proposed_fix: (1) Sign the Featured list and its log with curator keys, pinned in static config with a 2-of-3 threshold, and have wallets show Featured only when that check passes. (2) Require 2-of-2 directory signatures at launch: the Valar publisher plus an independently operated co-signer (for example Vizor) that re-checks handle-to-id for listed entries with its own X app, or at least refuses unexplained handle or avatar changes on listed entries. (3) Have wallets pin index→(handle, subject id) the first time they see it, and alert on changes for favourites and past delegations. (4) Ship the Phase 2 on-chain directory anchor at launch.

verdict.reasoning: Nothing a wallet can verify binds a handle, avatar or Featured status to a subject id. The overlay check covers only subject_commit against the (id, salt) pair in the registry doc and the DIK against the chain. Both are satisfied by an attacker's own legitimate entry relabelled as '@zooko', featured. Vizor's client-side lookalike check does not help, because it compares against handles in the same attacker-signed snapshot, and the real entry can be hidden or relabelled. There is partial detection: if the attacker has only KMS sign rights and bucket write, the real publisher's next seq collides and wallets raise an equivocation alarm within about 6 h. An attacker who controls the publisher host avoids that, and any delegation made in the window is final. The playbook's description of a forged snapshot as 'presentation-only lies' does not hold when delegation is final.
verdict.evidence: [doc] identity.md:913 ("presentation-only lies"), :642 and :897 (online KMS key used by the publisher), :685 (mirror is a pull-through cache), :617-633 (handles appear only in the profiles doc), :665-670 (overlay checks), :753-754 (curator approvals are off-chain); vizor.md:114-118 (client lookalike check uses snapshot data); client.md:608 (featured is display data).
verdict.refined_fix: (1) Wallets show Featured only when a curator-threshold signature (2-of-3, keys pinned in static config) over the featured list and log verifies. (2) Wallets pin index→(subject id, handle) on first sight for favourites and past delegations, and warn on any change. (3) Before launch, prefer an independently operated co-signer or auditor (for example Vizor's own X app) that re-checks handle↔id for listed entries. At minimum, ship the Phase 2 independent audit before the first proxy round.

findings.title: The X proof accepts any post by the account that contains the marker line, so an attacker can bind their own key to a famous account that merely posted or quoted that line
findings.description: The two-way binding is "the subject's post contains the DIK" plus "the DIK signs subject_commit". The parser looks only for a line-anchored marker anywhere in the post ("Other text is free"). The post can be a reply, any age, and posted in any context. If the target account ever posts that exact line (a scam warning, a reply that quotes it, or a post they were tricked into making), the attacker, who holds the DIK, gets a valid attestation. The entry is then shown with the target's handle, name and avatar, and becomes listed after 24 h.
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:141-142 (line-anchored regex, "exactly one distinct matched key"), :154 ("Only the marker line is parsed. Other text is free"), :488-493 (no recency or originality checks for REGISTER; recency applies only to recovery at :252).
findings.failure_scenario: @famous replies to a scammer with "Do not trust this key:\nzcash-vote-delegate v1 zvdk1<DIK_m>". The attacker resolves that post URL. author_id = @famous's id, the account is old and public, and exactly one key matches. The attacker signs `reg` with DIK_m and registers entry #N with subject @famous. After 24 h it is listed as "@famous" with their avatar, and delegations to it are final.
findings.proposed_fix: Require the whole post to match the template (only the claim sentence plus the marker, allowing whitespace). Require it to be an original post: not a reply, not a quote, not a repost. Require it to be created within, say, 7 days before the attestation. For accounts above a follower threshold, require manual review or an out-of-band confirmation before listing. Show the full post text on the resolve screen so the claimant confirms it.

verdict.reasoning: The parser accepts any post by the subject that contains a line-anchored marker, and the X fetch does not request referenced_tweets, so replies, quotes and retweets cannot be told apart. A stronger vector than the reply scenario [inference]: a v2 retweet is its own tweet object, with author_id set to the retweeter and text 'RT @orig: …'. If the attacker's post is 'x\nzcash-vote-delegate v1 zvdk1…', the marker sits on its own line in the retweet text, so a famous account that merely retweets it can be registered by the attacker. This is limited to subjects with no existing non-revoked entry, and the result is not featured (featured needs out-of-band confirmation). It can still be listed under the real handle and avatar after 24 h.
verdict.evidence: [doc] identity.md:141-142 (line-anchored regex, exactly one distinct key), :154 ("Other text is free"), :508 (tweet.fields has no referenced_tweets), :486-496 (no originality or recency checks for REGISTER; uniqueness only per subject), :252 (recency only for recovery), :804 (listing thresholds), :748 (featured needs out-of-band fingerprint confirmation).
verdict.refined_fix: Request `referenced_tweets` and require an original post (no reply, quote or retweet). Require the whole text to equal the template, modulo whitespace. Show the full post text on the resolve screen. Recency (for example ≤ 7 d before attestation) is optional; originality plus the full-template match close the hole.

findings.title: The DRK can cancel recoveries and (per the integrated design) unfreeze, so a DRK thief can lock the owner out for good; cancelled recoveries may also use up the 64-change cap
findings.description: (a) The DRK may cancel any pending change, including a verifier-attested recovery. Recovery exists for an owner who has lost the DIK. A thief who holds only the DRK can cancel every recovery the owner starts and keep routing every round. The verifier refuses to register the same X account again while a non-revoked entry exists, and the owner cannot revoke without the DIK. Coordinator suspension only kills the index, so the owner can never return under their X identity. (b) The integrated design lists `freeze`/`unfreeze` as DIK or DRK, which contradicts the identity spec ("Undone only by a route-key rotation (DIK)"). With DRK unfreeze, the owner's panic freeze can be undone by the very thief it is meant to stop. (c) The 64-change cap covers every key ever submitted, including burned pending keys. If cancelled recoveries count toward it, an X hijacker can repeat recover-then-cancel about 64 times at 3 a day. After that `rotate_route_key` is blocked forever, and a frozen entry can never be unfrozen. If they do not count, the reverse index grows without bound.
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:114 and :376 (recovery cancellable by the DRK, role 2), :116 (freeze undone only by DIK rotation), :370 (rotate requires key_change_count < max), :387 and :432 (burned pending keys indexed; 64-change cap), :493 (subject must have no non-revoked entry). integrated-design-v1.md:117 ("freeze / unfreeze (DIK or DRK)").
findings.failure_scenario: A delegate's phone is stolen with the DRK unlocked for the session, and the phrase was never backed up. The owner starts an X recovery, and the thief cancels it with the DRK every time. The thief routes rounds R1, R2 and onwards. Coordinators suspend #17. The owner's new registration under the same X account fails with SUBJECT_ALREADY_REGISTERED. Separately, a hijacker submits about 64 recoveries over 3 weeks and the owner cancels each one. Later the owner's DRK leaks: freeze works, but the owner can neither rotate nor unfreeze.
findings.proposed_fix: Only the DIK may cancel a RECOVERY. The DRK may cancel only co-signed changes. Unfreeze is DIK-only (rotation or an explicit DIK unfreeze). Count only changes that took effect toward max_key_changes. Track pending attempts separately and back them off (after an owner cancels a recovery, the subject cannot recover again for 30 d unless the DIK clears it). The verifier should allow the same subject to register again when the old entry is suspended for key compromise.

verdict.reasoning: (a) Confirmed. Recovery exists for an owner who has lost the DIK, yet the DRK may cancel it. A DRK thief can therefore block every recovery while routing, and suspension does not stop DRK cancels (cancel_pending has no suspension check). The owner is then stuck, because the verifier refuses re-registration while a non-revoked entry exists. A 7-day window is ample to fetch a cold DIK, so restricting RECOVER cancellation to the DIK costs little. (b) Confirmed as a document conflict: the integrated design says 'freeze / unfreeze (DIK or DRK)', while the identity spec has no unfreeze op and unfreezes only through a DIK rotation. (c) Mostly mitigated. Burned pending keys are indexed and the cap bounds that growth, so cancelled recoveries likely count. But each RECOVER needs a fresh verifier attestation (3 per 24 h per subject), and the playbook denylists the subject after a reported hijack, so about 64 cycles is unrealistic. A DIK thief can burn the cap with change/cancel loops, but that entry is lost to revoke anyway.
verdict.evidence: [doc] identity.md:114 and :376 (recovery cancellable by the DRK, role 2), :116 (freeze undone only by DIK rotation), :370 and :373 (cap checked on submission), :387 and :432 (burned keys indexed; 64-change cap), :482 (per-subject rate limit), :131 (verifier denylists the subject), :493 (no re-registration while a non-revoked entry exists). integrated-design-v1.md:117.
verdict.refined_fix: Allow only the DIK to cancel a RECOVERY pending change; the DRK may still cancel co-signed changes. Fix the integrated design to read: freeze by DIK or DRK; unfreeze only through a DIK rotation. Verifier policy: after an owner cancels a recovery, refuse RECOVER for that subject for 30 d. Allow, after manual review, re-registration of a subject whose entry is suspended for reason 2 (key compromise).

findings.title: Theft of the hot route key steals every unrouted proposal in every active round at once; the DIK/DRK split does not prevent this, and in Vizor the DIK is not actually kept offline
findings.description: Routes are one-shot, immediate and accepted until vote_end. A thief with the DRK routes all unrouted proposals of all active rounds in one tx per round, before any rotation or freeze can land. The specs present the split as damage limitation ("at most route this round's un-routed proposals"), but that limit is already the maximum possible damage. In Vizor both keys come from one phrase stored on the same device, with the DRK unlocked for the whole session. So the split protects identity continuity, not delegators' weight. Owner decision 2 makes delegations final, but nothing requires routes to take effect immediately.
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:102 (DRK unlocked for the session), :99-103 (root and DRK in the same app secure store), :123 ("at most route this round's un-routed proposals"), :129. integrated-design-v1.md:124 (routes accepted until vote_end_time), :41 (one-shot).
findings.failure_scenario: On day 6 of a 7-day round, malware or a backup leak exposes the DRK. One MsgDelegateRoute per active round routes all 50 unrouted proposals against the delegate's public stance. The owner's rotate lands one block later, and the routes stand.
findings.proposed_fix: Materially better alternative: a route takes effect Δ (for example 2 h) after inclusion. During Δ a DIK-signed `veto_route` can void it, after which the delegate can route that proposal again. Routes must land by vote_end − Δ, so every route is final by vote_end. At minimum, store the DRK with per-use user presence (it already needs re-auth per route), not session unlock, and correct the damage-limitation claim in the spec.

verdict.reasoning: The spec's bound ('at most route this round's un-routed proposals') is accurate. It compares DIK theft with DRK theft and does not claim that the split protects weight, so the finding mostly restates an accepted risk. The same exposure already exists for a voter's session-unlocked voting hotkey today, though a delegate's key carries pooled weight. The delayed-route-with-DIK-veto alternative is not clearly better. It adds an earlier effective deadline, it requires the owner to watch within Δ, and it gives a DIK thief a tool to veto honest routes. One cheap, real inconsistency remains: routes already require re-auth per use, yet the DRK is stored session-unlocked.
verdict.evidence: [doc] identity.md:102 (DRK session-unlocked), :123 (damage bound), :129; integrated-design-v1.md:41 (route needs re-auth plus a confirm sheet), :124.
verdict.refined_fix: Store the DRK behind per-use user presence (Keychain/Keystore access control), matching the existing per-route re-auth. Reword the spec to say the DIK/DRK split protects identity continuity, not weight already pooled. Do not adopt delayed routes by default.

findings.title: Signed-message formats for the registry and routes differ across the component specs, and some leave out the chain or the key epoch, which allows replays (including after a chain reset that keeps the same chain id)
findings.description: The integrated design adopts the identity spec's DIK/DRK operations but leaves the signed digests (the 32-byte hashes each key signs) unreconciled. Identity: `net` string, plain u32 fields, and the `route` digest has no network or chain binding. Chain: `lp8(chain_id)`, 32-byte padded fields, D3-D7 for a single key. Client: route digest without chain or key_epoch; rotate digest `SVOTE_DELEGATE_ROTATE_V1‖d‖old‖new` without chain or epoch; directory signature over `...:v1\0‖sha256(json)`, against the identity spec's `...:v1\n‖payload`. Rollout: `chain_id‖round‖d‖dk`. The domain `SVOTE_DELEGATE_ROUTE_V1` has at least two different layouts. Binding chain_id alone is also not enough: production resets wipe state and reuse the same chain id, and no registry export step exists. The same phrase re-derives the same DIK at i=0, so old public revoke or freeze txs can replay against a re-registered entry that lands on the same index. After such a reset, indices also point to different people. Key derivation has no network input, so mainnet and testnet keys are identical.
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:183-203 (route digest without net), :88-89 (derivation without network); chain.md:338-357; client.md:577, :591, :614; spec_rollout.md:245. [code] scripts/init.sh:16 (CHAIN_ID defaults to svote-1); docs/production-setup.md:101-110 (reset wipes state, fresh genesis). [measured] review-identity/domains.py: all 24 domain strings across specs and sighash.go are prefix-free, but SVOTE_DELEGATE_ROUTE_V1 is defined twice with different layouts.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) The chain is built from chain.md D7 and the client from client.md §4.4, so every route fails to verify on the day the feature activates. (b) A beta registry is reset by the documented workflow. A delegate restores from the phrase, re-registers, and lands on index 3 with the same DIK. Anyone replays the old chain's public `revoke{3, epoch 0}` and the entry is permanently REVOKED. Old links /d/3 without k= open a different person.
findings.proposed_fix: Write one normative digest table in ZIP-DR. Every digest binds chain_id plus a random `registry_instance_id` fixed at registry genesis and preserved on export/import, plus u64 key_epoch and index. Publish cross-language vectors (Go, Rust, e2e) and a unit test asserting that all SVOTE_ domain constants are prefix-free. Add the network to the key derivation personalisation. Make the reset runbook export and import the registry (and fail closed without it). Make the k= fingerprint in deep links mandatory.

verdict.reasoning: The digest inconsistency is real. The route digest has four different layouts: identity has no chain binding, chain D7 uses lp8(chain_id) and a u64 epoch, client uses a different domain and includes the DK, and rollout has its own. The integrated design adopts the identity ops but never fixes a normative table. However, the shared crate and cross-language vectors, plus the T1-T3 stage rounds, would catch a mismatch long before mainnet, so 'every route fails on activation day' is not realistic. The replay-after-reset scenario is largely refuted. The identity spec already requires exporting and importing all 0x1A state across resets. The verifier also refuses a DIK already in its store, so the same-phrase re-registration that the replay needs is blocked unless the verifier DB is wiped too. Cross-network route replay would need an identical round_id, which is derived from the creation height, snapshot and proposals.
verdict.evidence: [doc] identity.md:203 (route digest has no net), :443 (genesis export/import of 0x1A required), :494 (verifier refuses a DIK seen in its store); chain.md:338-357 (D3-D7, single DK, lp8(chain_id)); client.md:577, :591, :614; spec_rollout.md:245. [code] x/vote/keeper/msg_server.go:401-409 (round_id = Poseidon(createdAtHeight, snapshot, proposals, end time, roots)); docs/production-setup.md:101-110 (current reset uses a fresh genesis).
verdict.refined_fix: Add one normative digest table to ZIP-DR, based on the identity layouts the integrated design adopts. Add chain_id (or net) to the route digest, and put all digests in the shared crate's vectors (Go and Rust). Add a fail-closed step to the reset runbook that exports and imports 0x1A state. A registry instance id and network-specific key derivation are optional.

findings.title: The per-block cap on registry ops does not de-duplicate or prioritise, so floods of cheap conflicting ops can keep defensive ops (cancel, revoke, freeze) out of blocks
findings.description: Registry ops and routes are free and authenticated by Ed25519 signatures, which cost nothing to make. CheckTx runs only the ante handler against committed state, not the message handler, so many conflicting ops that are each valid against that state all enter the mempool. Examples are thousands of `rotate_route_key` variants with different new_drk at the same epoch, or route variants for the same proposal. The identity spec caps registry ops at 64 per block by "following the precedent", but that precedent de-duplicates on a round-scoped nullifier key, and no equivalent key is defined here. The chain spec says no cap is needed for routes.
findings.evidence: [code] app/vote_share_submission_proposal.go:29-58 (precedent de-duplicates by (round, nullifier) before the cap); app/ante.go:117-160 (vote txs get ante validation only; the SDK does not run msg handlers in CheckTx) [inference on SDK]. [doc] identity.md:434; chain.md:617.
findings.failure_scenario: A delegate whose DIK was stolen (or a sybil delegate, see IDN-10) signs 5,000 rotate variants every epoch. PrepareProposal fills the 64 slots first-in first-out: one succeeds and 63 fail. Recheck evicts the stale ones, and the attacker re-signs for the new epoch. Meanwhile another owner's `cancel_pending` cannot reach a block before their hostile recovery's effective_time.
findings.proposed_fix: In PrepareProposal and ProcessProposal keep at most one registry op per delegate_index per block (per new DIK for register) and one route per (round, d). Give revoke, cancel_pending and freeze a reserved share of the cap, placed before rotate, register and recover. Consider a CheckTx in-flight cache keyed by (index, epoch).

verdict.reasoning: The design gap is real. A global per-block cap of 64 registry ops copies the reveal precedent without its dedupe key. Ed25519 variants are nearly free to produce (change_identity and rotate variants with fresh keys are all valid against committed state), and routes have neither a cap nor a per-(round, d) dedupe. Starving a defensive op for a 7 d or 72 h window is impractical, though. CometBFT's mempool and this chain's PrepareProposal keep FIFO order, and recheck re-runs the stateful checks, so all of an entry's stale variants are evicted after one lands. An honest cancel is delayed by about as many blocks as the attacker has entries with preloaded variants (minutes), not days. What remains is block-space and mempool griefing.
verdict.evidence: [code] app/vote_share_submission_proposal.go:29-58 (dedupe by (round, nullifier) before the cap); app/ante.go:117-160 (custom ante); x/vote/ante/validate.go:33-36,137-140 (recheck still runs state checks). [doc] identity.md:434 (cap 'following the precedent'); chain.md:606 (chain spec had a 10-min per-delegate key-change interval, not carried into the integrated design), :617 (no cap for routes), :619.
verdict.refined_fix: In PrepareProposal and ProcessProposal keep at most one registry op per delegate_index per block, and one route tx per (round, d) per block, mirroring the nullifier dedupe. Alternatively drop the global 64 cap, since Ed25519 is cheap. Keep the chain spec's minimum interval between key changes per delegate.

findings.title: Any subdomain of one domain counts as a separate DNS subject with no age gate, so one domain yields unlimited sybil delegates and can use up the verifier's daily cap
findings.description: A DNS subject is any FQDN that is a registrable domain or a subdomain of one. The DNS registration gate is only "consistent resolution". With wildcard DNS and TLS (the HTTPS .well-known method) or a DNS API, one domain produces unlimited distinct subjects. Per-subject and per-IP limits do not bind these, and the global cap of 500 attestations a day is shared with X registrations. The result is free registry spam, sybils for the IDN-9 flood, and an onboarding denial of service for real delegates, for example just before a round.
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:181 (subdomains allowed), :803 (DNS gate: "Consistent resolution"), :481-485 (per-subject, per-IP and global 500/day limits).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with evil.example and 50 proxy IPs serves `https://aN.evil.example/.well-known/zcash-vote-delegate.json` dynamically and requests 500 attestations a day. Legitimate X delegates get RATE_LIMITED the day before the first proxy round.
findings.proposed_fix: Treat the registrable domain (eTLD+1) as the DNS subject for uniqueness and rate limits, or allow DNS registration only for registrable domains. Give each provider its own quota so DNS and GitHub cannot starve X. Count failed and unused issuances against the IP and its /24.

verdict.reasoning: Any subdomain is a distinct DNS subject, and the DNS registration gate is only 'consistent resolution', so one domain yields unlimited subjects that per-subject limits do not bind. Issuances count against a single global daily cap of 500 shared with X. A few IPs at 10 per hour each can exhaust it, and unused issuances still count. Severity is lower than stated for two reasons. DNS entries are never listed unless featured, so the sybils are lookup-only. And this is off-chain verifier policy that can be changed within hours without touching the chain.
verdict.evidence: [doc] identity.md:181 (subdomains allowed), :803-804 (DNS gate is consistent resolution; DNS listed only if featured), :481-485 (per-subject, per-IP, per-DIK and global 500/day limits), :807 (thresholds are off-chain policy).
verdict.refined_fix: Use the registrable domain (eTLD+1) for DNS uniqueness and rate limits; subject_commit can stay on the FQDN. Give each provider its own quota, and count unused issuances against the IP and its /24.

findings.title: Lookalike checks favour whoever registered first and ignore handle history, Featured is empty for the first 30 days, and successor links let a hijacker inherit a retired delegate's reputation
findings.description: Lookalike flags compare against Featured handles and handles of entries registered earlier, and "the older or Featured entry is never flagged". Handles are mutable. An early registrant can later rename to a skeleton of a newer real person's handle, and the real person is the one flagged. Handles that change owner (deactivation after 30 days, the X Handle Marketplace) are treated as safe because binding is by numeric id. But a new subject who now holds a well-known handle is not flagged on its own entry. Featured requires 30 days of registration, so at launch the display-name and avatar checks (Featured-only) protect nothing. The "re-registered as #N" predecessor link is inferred from the same subject, so whoever controls the X account after the owner revokes inherits the old entry's following.
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:784 and vizor.md:118 (precedence by registration order), :787-791 (names and avatars compared only with Featured), :745 (Featured needs ≥30 d), :833 (handle reassignment called safe), :621 and :130 (predecessor or successor link).
findings.failure_scenario: The attacker registers #5 as @benign. The real @zooko registers #50, and is not Featured until day 30. The attacker renames to @zook0, so #50 (the real one) shows "Looks similar to @zook0". Or: @trusted_old retires, and the marketplace assigns that handle to the attacker's new account, which registers and appears as "@trusted_old" with no warning.
findings.proposed_fix: Decide precedence by when the directory first saw each (skeleton, subject) pair, not by registration index. Re-check lookalikes on every handle change and flag the entry that renamed. Reserve skeletons seen on any entry in the last 12 months and add "handle previously used by #N". Seed a reserved-names list of known ecosystem accounts at launch. Gate the rollout on the registry being live at least 30 days, with Featured seeded, before the first proxy round. Publish successor links only from a DIK-signed successor statement or after curator review.

verdict.reasoning: Precedence comes from registration order, while handles are mutable. An early registrant can rename to a lookalike of a later real person, and the real person is the one flagged. Both the server and the client rules say the older entry is never flagged. A new subject that acquires a retired or deactivated handle is not compared with hidden or revoked entries, so it gets no warning. Featured requires 30 days of registration. The rollout has featured delegates register only after the coordinated activation and then moves straight to the first public proxy round, so Featured, and with it the display-name and avatar checks, would be empty at launch. The predecessor/successor mechanism is unspecified. If it is inferred from the subject, whoever controls the X account later inherits the link.
verdict.evidence: [doc] identity.md:784 (featured or listed handles registered earlier), :787-791 (names and avatars compared only with featured), :745 (registered ≥ 30 d), :833 (reassignment called safe), :130 and :622 (successor/predecessor link, mechanism unspecified); vizor.md:117-118 (older or featured entry never flagged); spec_rollout.md:521-535 and :840 (featured registered after activation, no 30-day gate before the first proxy round).
verdict.refined_fix: Decide lookalike precedence by when the directory first saw each (skeleton, subject) pair. Re-run the check on every handle change and flag the entry that renamed. Keep a 12-month reservation of skeletons with 'handle previously used by #N'. Either gate the first proxy round on the registry being live for at least 30 days, or let ecosystem-role featured entries skip the 30-day wait with out-of-band fingerprint confirmation. Publish successor links only from a DIK-signed statement or after curator review.

findings.title: The X data-deletion plan (crypto-shredding) does not work: salts and X ids are published to every wallet and kept indefinitely, so an X account linked to a delegate can still be identified after deletion
findings.description: The spec claims that deleting the salt makes the on-chain subject_commit unlinkable. But every registry doc publishes subject.id and salt. Those docs are content-addressed objects that are never stated to be deleted, and every wallet caches them. Wallets also keep `handle_at_delegation` or `display_handle` indefinitely. After a purge, anyone with an older doc can recompute the commit and link the on-chain entry, and its public routes, to the deleted X account. Purging on ACCOUNT_GONE also covers temporary X suspensions, which permanently removes the ability to recover through X. Smaller policy items for counsel: record off-X-matching consent; pairing X profiles with a public governance voting record may fall under X's restrictions on sensitive or political profiling; redistributing the profiles doc to other wallets (open question 6).
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:274-275 (crypto-shredding claim), :617-625 (registry entry carries "subject":{"id","salt"}), :589-592 (purge scope: next doc only), :674 (wallet persists handle_at_delegation); client.md:635 (display_handle kept); dossier identity_research.md:197-199 (24 h deletion duty, keep content current).
findings.failure_scenario: Alice deletes her X account. The verifier purges her id and salt within 24 h, but registry docs seq ≤ N on the CDN, mirror caches and every wallet still hold {id, salt}. An analyst recomputes subject_commit and attributes entry #17's routes to Alice's deleted account.
findings.proposed_fix: On purge, delete the historical registry and profile objects and purge the CDN. Have wallets drop subject ids from caches once a doc expires. Store the handle with an expiry, or only the index and fingerprint. Describe crypto-shredding as best-effort against archivers. Keep a keyed-hash tombstone so subject uniqueness survives a purge. Do not purge on temporary suspension until the X account has been gone for N days. Record DIK-signed consent and get counsel sign-off on the political-profiling question.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed: the purge covers DB fields, avatars and only the next registry doc. Historical content-addressed registry and profiles objects are never stated to be deleted, so the bucket and CDN keep subject id, salt and handles, an X compliance gap for developer-stored data. Calling crypto-shredding 'unlinkable' is overstated, because the salt was published to everyone. Partly refuted: the client spec keeps only the latest snapshot and purges on refresh, so wallets do not retain old docs, apart from the user's own handle_at_delegation and display_handle records. The incremental privacy harm is small, since the delegate's handle-to-entry link was public while they were active. Purging the salt also has a real side effect the finding only hints at: the verifier loses the ability to check subject uniqueness and recovery for that entry. Its 'don't purge on temporary suspension' fix may conflict with X's rule to remove content that is no longer available.

findings.title: The identity and Vizor specs disagree on the user-generated-content controls that App Store and Google Play require

The identity spec gives: a report web form opened in an external browser, no in-app block, 500-character statements with a URL, and no text-moderation state for listed entries. The Vizor spec gives: in-app report via POST to functions.vizor.cash, a local "Hide delegate", a 160-character bio with no links, and display gated on `text_status == approved`, which the identity service never produces. The integrated design lists only "a report form".

findings.title: The delegate key phrase is a standard 24-word BIP-39 phrase that cannot be told apart from a wallet seed
findings.description: Asking users to create, back up and type a second 24-word BIP-39 phrase for delegate profiles teaches them to enter 24 words into delegate flows, which helps phishing. It also allows mix-ups: backing up the wrong phrase, or restoring a wallet seed as the delegate phrase, which copies the seed into a second store whose derived DRK is kept unlocked for the session. The format must be fixed before launch because changing it later breaks existing backups.
findings.evidence: [doc] identity.md:86 (BIP-39, 24 words, English, empty passphrase), :100-101 (root entropy in app secure storage); integrated-design-v1.md:191, :260 (O4 picks the phrase).
findings.failure_scenario: A fake site, "Restore your Zcash delegate key phrase to keep your listing", collects 24-word phrases, and users paste wallet seeds. Or a user backs up only the delegate phrase, believing it is the wallet's.
findings.proposed_fix: Use a typed phrase that a wallet seed cannot pass for. Options: an Electrum-style version prefix check, a different word count with a domain-separated checksum, or a non-BIP-39 encoding. Explicitly reject phrases that validate as a wallet seed in delegate restore. Add copy saying "This is not your wallet recovery phrase; never enter your wallet phrase here."

verdict.reasoning: Real: a second, ordinary 24-word BIP-39 phrase cannot be told apart from a Zcash wallet seed, which invites mix-ups and gives phishers a pretext. The format must be fixed before launch. The impact is overstated, though. Entering a wallet seed as the delegate phrase stores it behind re-auth, the same protection the mnemonic already has, and the session-unlocked DRK is a one-way BLAKE2b output that does not expose the seed. Restore would simply find no matching entry. The proposed 'reject phrases that validate as a wallet seed' cannot work while the delegate phrase is itself BIP-39.

verdict.refined_fix: Use a phrase format that BIP-39 wallets reject and that wallet seeds fail, for example an Electrum-style version prefix or checksum, or a non-BIP-39 encoding. Delegate restore then rejects wallet seeds deterministically. Add copy that says this is not the wallet recovery phrase.

findings.title: No single Ed25519 verification rule is specified, and keys with a small-order component pass the proposed key check, so the chain and independent verifiers can disagree about signatures
findings.description: The identity spec says the chain verifies with Go stdlib `crypto/ed25519`. The chain spec says CometBFT ZIP-215. zcash_voting uses ed25519-dalek `verify`. ZIP-215 and the stricter RFC 8032 check that Go stdlib and dalek use differ on keys and R values that carry a small-order (torsion) component. The proposed `ValidateDelegateKey` rejects only small-order keys. A malicious delegate can register a key with a torsion component and produce public routes that the chain accepts but auditors using stdlib or dalek reject. The delegate can then disown those routes, and verifier-side checks diverge from chain-side checks. Divergence also arises from R values with a torsion component even when the key is clean, so one rule must be used everywhere. Consensus determinism is not at risk, since all validators run the same code.

[doc] identity.md:65,77; chain.md:70-75. findings.failure_scenario: A delegate registers a DIK and DRK with a torsion component. All of their routes land on chain. An independent audit tool built on stdlib or dalek reports about half of them as having invalid signatures, and the delegate claims those routes were forged.
findings.proposed_fix: Make ZIP-215 normative in ZIP-DR for every delegate and verifier signature: CometBFT/curve25519-voi in Go, ed25519-zebra or ed25519-consensus in Rust (verifier crate, wallet, audit CLI). Also require keys with no small-order component at registration ([L]A = identity) as extra protection. Add test vectors covering keys and R values with a small-order component.

findings.title: Deep links put the delegate index in the URL path, the key check is optional, and the fingerprint and identicon are weaker than the trust placed in them
findings.description: The integrated design's link `link.vizor.cash/d/<index>#k=…` puts the index in the path. Users without the app installed, and desktop users, send it to the deep-link server and CDN logs together with their IP. That contradicts the design's rule that a delegator never reveals which index they are interested in, and the identity spec's fragment-only design. In Vizor `k` is optional, and a mismatch shows only a banner. Fingerprint definitions conflict: the identity spec uses a 60-bit hash, Vizor the first 80 bits of the key's bech32 string. The identicon carries about 20 bits, so an impostor key matching the identicon and the first fingerprint group costs about 2^40 key generations, which a laptop can do.

Block the Delegate button on a mismatch until the user acknowledges it. Define one fingerprint (prefer the 80-bit prefix of the bech32 key). Present identicons as decoration, not as verification.

findings.title: The new `unfreeze` op makes registry freezes replayable, and the global registry-op cap can then be griefed
findings.description: The integrated design adds `freeze / unfreeze (DIK or DRK)` to MsgDelegateRegistry and a single global per-block cap on registry ops. The identity spec has no unfreeze: leaving FROZEN takes the 72 h change_identity path, which bumps key_epoch. Its freeze digest is `net || index || key_epoch` with no nonce, and its only replay protection is that key changes bump key_epoch. Custom-wire txs have no account sequence. If unfreeze leaves key_epoch unchanged, every freeze or unfreeze tx a delegate has signed becomes valid again after the opposite op lands. Anyone can rebroadcast it once the CometBFT mempool LRU cache (default 10,000 entries, not overridden by svoted) has evicted its hash, which takes about a minute of normal reveal traffic. Three further problems: (a) letting the DRK unfreeze defeats freeze as a response to DRK compromise; (b) toggles are fee-less and unbounded, so one registered delegate can fill the shared `max_registry_ops_per_block` (64) in every block, starving other delegates' time-critical ops (cancel_pending during a 7-day hostile recovery, revoke, freeze); (c) registry digests bind a 3-valued `net` (main/test/regtest), not the vote chain ID. Ops therefore replay across chains that share `net`: a mainnet chain reset (zvote-1 to zvote-2 with exported state), the rehearsal network, or a stage chain configured as "main".

[code] app/ante.go:120-129 (custom vote txs: infinite gas meter, no signer account or sequence); cmd/svoted/cmd/commands.go:47-51 (only consensus/P2P timeouts overridden, so mempool cache_size stays at the CometBFT default 10000). [inference] CometBFT never checks committed txs against the block store for duplicates.
findings.failure_scenario: A delegate freezes at epoch 0 after a scare, finds no compromise, and unfreezes (still epoch 0). Close to vote_end_time, an attacker rebroadcasts the original freeze bytes, which are valid again because status is ACTIVE and the epoch is unchanged. The delegate's late MsgDelegateRoute txs fail with "delegate not ACTIVE". If the delegate unfreezes again, the attacker re-replays the freeze in the next block. Every proposal the delegate had not yet routed abstains, so the whole pool is suppressed. In a separate attack, a single delegate toggles freeze and unfreeze 32 times per block, which blocks other delegates' cancel_pending and lets a hostile 7-day recovery mature.
findings.proposed_fix: Preferred: drop `unfreeze` and keep the identity-spec semantics, where FROZEN is left only through change_identity, which bumps key_epoch. If unfreeze stays, make it DIK-only and have every registry op increment a per-record `op_seq` that every registry digest includes. Bind ctx.ChainID() (not only `net`) into all registry and route digests, as chain.md D3-D7 did. Replace or supplement the global cap with a per-delegate rate limit, for example a stored last_op_height, and exempt or reserve capacity for revoke, freeze and cancel_pending. Add replay tests that rebroadcast committed registry txs after cache eviction.

verdict.reasoning:
The core claim holds. The integrated design adds an `unfreeze` op (DIK or DRK) that is not specified anywhere. The identity spec is replay-safe only because it has no unfreeze: a delegate leaves FROZEN only through change_identity or recover, and Effective() bumps key_epoch on that path, so an old freeze can never apply again. If unfreeze leaves the epoch unchanged, the freeze digest (net, index, key_epoch, no nonce) becomes valid again. Custom-wire txs have no sequence and the app keeps no tx-hash replay set, so a rebroadcast after mempool-cache eviction or a node restart lands. (a) is also real: if the DRK can unfreeze, freezing in response to a DRK compromise does nothing.

Two sub-claims are overstated. (b) A 7-day starvation of cancel_pending does not hold. The cap precedent leaves over-limit txs in the mempool, and PrepareProposal handles txs in CometBFT's FIFO reap order, so new attacker ops queue behind the victim's op. Recheck also evicts ops that state has made invalid, such as extra freezes once the delegate is FROZEN. The delay is bounded to minutes. A related problem is real, though. CheckTx runs only the ante, so a delegate can sign one digest many times with fresh Ed25519 nonces. Those distinct valid txs all pass CheckTx and can fill the 64-op cap, or the mempool, until the next commit. Without unfreeze this is bounded per delegate (one freeze plus at most 64 key changes); with an epoch-preserving unfreeze it is unbounded. (c) Binding `net` instead of the chain ID is a real inconsistency with chain.md and spec_rollout, but it matters little without unfreeze: an exported reset carries epochs, statuses and used attestation ids, so replays fail. Overall this is a design gap to close before implementation, not a shipped hole, so medium.
